newsitem.title: USA: Profiles of Middle East leaders at U.S. summit.
newsitem.headline: Profiles of Middle East leaders at U.S. summit.

text.p: Brief profiles of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and King Hussein of Jordan, who will attend a U.S.-sponsored summit in Washington this week.
The talks are intended to salvage the Middle East peace process, which threatened to unravel after Israeli-Palestinian violence last week claimed the lives of nearly 70 people.
Following are brief profiles of the three leaders.

ISRAELI PRIME MINISTER BENJAMIN NETANYAHU, tested by fire, has ended his first 100 days as Israel's prime minister by rushing to Washington to try to put out new flames of Palestinian fury. The right-wing Israeli leader insists his initial three months in office, during which he met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat after long expressing reluctance to do so, show he is a peacemaker.

Palestinians accuse him of foot-dragging by failing to implement peace deals they signed with the previous Labour-led government, especially an Israeli promise to pull troops out of many parts of the West Bank city of Hebron.

The West Bank, Gaza Strip and Arab East Jerusalem erupted in rage last week after Netanyahu opened an archaeological tunnel near Moslem shrines. Netanyahu, 46, sent tanks to the West Bank and Gaza and said the tunnel would remain open.

Netanyahu was elected prime minister last May on a platform ruling out swapping land-for-peace with Arabs or making any concessions on Israeli-occupied Arab Jersualem, which Palestinians view as the capital of a future Palestinian state. He also kept a pledge to expand Jewish settlement in the West Bank -- sparking Palestinian fury and international condemnation.

Born in Tel Aviv to an eminent historian, he spent much of his early life in the United States. He was in an elite Israeli army unit from 1967 to 1972. He was shot leading commandos disguised as workers onto a commandeered Sabena airliner in 1972.

PALESTINIAN PRESIDENT YASSER ARAFAT won international sympathy against the hardline policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu but faces a tougher battle for the independent state that is his dream.

Describing Netanyahu's policies as "idiotic," Arafat accused Israel last week of declaring war on Palestinians by reneging on peace commitments, tampering with Moslem holy places in Arab East Jerusalem and expanding Jewish settlements.
Palestinian frustrations exploded into protests that led to gunbattles between Israeli soldiers and Palestinian policemen in which about 70 people were killed.

Arafat's aspirations for an independent Palestinian state were dealt a blow when Israeli voters chose Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud party, over Labour Prime Minister Shimon Peres in May elections.
Arafat, head of the Palestine Liberation Organisation, was born in Cairo on August 24, 1929 and has spent most of his adult life fighting for a Palestinian state.

"The thing that keeps me going, the most precious thing that is always on my mind, is the regaining of dignity for the Palestinian people, and restoring the name of Palestine to the map of the Middle East," he says.
JORDANIAN KING HUSSEIN's triumph was a peace treaty that ended Jordan's nearly half a century of war with Israel after a lifetime manoeuvring in the shifting sands of Middle East politics.

Through wars, assassination attempts, civil unrest and official hostility to Israel, King Hussein, 60, repeatedly turned to secret contacts with the Jewish state. They finally burst into the open and a formal peace treaty was signed on the Israeli-Jordanian border on October 26, 1994.
The third king in the Hashemite dynasty to rule Jordan often seems the only force holding the country together.

His recurring internal problem has been relations with the Palestinians. Although Israel took the West Bank from him in the 1967 Middle East war, Palestinians suspected he harboured dreams of resuming his rule even after he formally abandoned claims to the West Bank in 1988.

Internationally, King Hussein continually shifted alliances, outlasting every other leader in the Middle East. He fought tank battles with invading Syrian forces in 1970, alternated icy and warm relations with Egypt and moved close to Iraq in the 1980s, only to distance himself after the 1991 Gulf War.
